jetstore-owned-asset.name: data_model/jets_agentic.meta.json
jetstore-owned-asset.note: Installed into this workspace at image build time and overwritten on every build; a local edit is lost, and the build fails rather than clobbering it silently. Extend the model from your own file that imports this one.

jetsa:AgentRun.description: One execution of one agent: the unit the audit store correlates on (its run_id) and the carrier of the reproducibility fields the proposal's generated_by block names.

jetsa:run_id.description: The run identity; agent_audit.run_id correlates to it.

jetsa:agent_version.description: The agent's version, for reproducibility (the proposal's generated_by).

jetsa:model_id.description: The model that served the run.

jetsa:tier.description: The autonomy tier the run executed under, recorded not enforced.

jetsa:ended_at.description: When the run ended; unset while running.

jetsa:run_status.description: The run outcome: succeeded, exhausted, interrupted or failed; unset while running (class-scoped: status is the proposal's name on Incident). The budget running out is 'exhausted' rather than a failure - it is the compile-pass rate's denominator - and 'interrupted' is the wall-clock cap, distinguished from a caller's cancellation.

jetsa:triggered_by.description: What started the run: a schedule, an anomaly, a user (class-scoped: trigger_ref is the proposal's name on ChangeProposal).

jetsa:domain_model_version.description: The domain model version the run reasoned against.

jetsa:iteration_cap.description: Maximum propose-verify-repair iterations before the run ends as exhausted.

jetsa:wall_clock_cap_seconds.description: Maximum wall-clock seconds for the whole run, carried on the run's context; the only cap that bounds a call the request timeout missed.

jetsa:token_spend.description: Total tokens consumed by the run, accumulated from the inference responses; unset while running. Recorded rather than capped - it is what lets the eval harness compare sampling policies at equal spend.

jetsa:ApprovalEvent.description: One human or agent decision on a supervised subject: the supervision seam. Outcomes are appended, never updated — a decision is a new event referencing the same subject.

jetsa:run_ref.description: The AgentRun this event belongs to (class-scoped: run_id names the run's own identity).

jetsa:subject_ref.description: The Remediation or ChangeProposal being decided.

jetsa:from_state.description: The approval state before the decision.

jetsa:to_state.description: The approval state after the decision.

jetsa:actor.description: Who decided: a user_email or an agent identity.

jetsa:tier_at_event.description: The autonomy tier at the time of the event (class-scoped).

jetsa:decision_rationale.description: Why, in the actor's words (class-scoped: rationale is the proposal's name on ChangeProposal).

jetsa:ChangeProposal.description: A proposed code or configuration change (the proposal's ChangeProposal), flattened to scalar and array properties: code_diff, ci_result and impact_analysis are nested objects in the schema and JetRules has no anonymous nested object.

jetsa:trigger.description: What prompted the proposal (the proposal's ChangeTrigger vocabulary; carried as text — the vocabulary ships with its consumer).

jetsa:trigger_ref.description: Incident, drift detection, or backlog item.

jetsa:code_diff_files_changed.description: code_diff.files_changed of the proposal's ChangeProposal. Optional: it was once declared list[str] with default=None, which Pydantic does not validate and which the DDL emitter read as required-and-defaulted-to-null - two claims that cannot both hold. The default says the intent was optional.

jetsa:assumptions_made.description: The assumptions the proposal rests on. Optional, for the same reason as code_diff_files_changed.

jetsa:generated_tests.description: The tests generated with the change (min 1).

jetsa:approval_state.description: Where the proposal sits in the approval lifecycle.

jetsa:proposal_model_version.description: The domain model version the proposal was generated against (class-scoped; domain_model_version stays on AgentRun).

jetsa:Anomaly.description: A deterministic detector's observation (the proposal's Anomaly), a table. Widened from the skeleton to what the anomaly design says the execution record can actually populate. **The field list is derived from the detectors' six derivable rows, not from readability.** Every property below is populated by at least one of them; two of the proposal's optional properties are left out because none of the six can populate them: - `confidence` — the proposal has it optional. All six rows are predicates or windowed aggregates over a relational table, so a detector emits a fact and has no calibrated confidence to report. Adding it would invite a constant. **Its consumer is the Observer agent, not a detector.** - `correlation_group_id` — the proposal says *"Assigned by Observer Agent"*, so by construction no deterministic detector writes it. Clustering anomalies into an Incident is `Incident.hypotheses`' side of the model. Both are recorded here rather than silently dropped. **Three of the proposal's required properties are optional here**, because the detector rows fix which rows carry a number: `expected_min`, `expected_max` and `deviation_magnitude` exist for rows 1 and 3, which compare against a history window, and do not exist for rows 2, 4, 5 and 10, which are within-run predicates with no range and no magnitude. Requiring them would force a detector to invent one. **Names are class-scoped, named against the namespace rather than for readability.** `subject_ref` is a hard collision — it is ApprovalEvent's, declared there first — and `signal_type`, `observed_value`, `detector_ref` and `session_id` are exactly the generic names a client workspace would want for something else. Each carries its proposal name in its description, per the model's documented-against rule.

jetsa:anomaly_session_id.description: The pipeline run the observation is drawn from - `session_id` on every table of the execution record, and the key `purge_database` deletes by. Class-scoped, and deliberately not named run_ref: that is ApprovalEvent's and means an AgentRun, which this is not.

jetsa:anomaly_subject_type.description: What the observation is about (the proposal names it subject_ref.entity_type). The detectors' grain: worker for rows 1-4, edge for rows 2, 5 and 10.

jetsa:anomaly_subject_ref.description: The subject's identity (the proposal names it subject_ref.entity_id; class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's subject_ref, which is a Remediation or ChangeProposal). For a worker, the step label, shard and jets_partition that key the row; for an edge, those plus the input and output channel.

jetsa:anomaly_signal_type.description: Which failure mode was observed (the proposal names it signal_type). Maps to a detector row: rejection_rate is row 1, volume is rows 2 and 5, step_regression row 3, worker_stall row 4, arrival row 10.

jetsa:anomaly_observed_value.description: What was measured (the proposal names it observed_value). **Text because the proposal types it [number, string] and JetRules has no union**, and because the detector rows genuinely differ: a ratio for row 1, a count for rows 2 and 5, a status for rows 3 and 4, a destination URI for row 10. The trigger property on ChangeProposal is carried as text for the same reason.

jetsa:anomaly_expected_min.description: The low end of what was expected (the proposal names it expected_range.min; text on the same reasoning as observed_value). Optional rather than required as the proposal has it: only rows 1 and 3 compare against a range at all.

jetsa:anomaly_expected_max.description: The high end of what was expected (the proposal names it expected_range.max). Optional, same reasoning as expected_min.

jetsa:anomaly_expected_basis.description: **What the observation was compared against** (the proposal names it expected_range.basis) - the history window and grouping for rows 1 and 3, the within-run invariant for rows 2, 4 and 5, the claim being checked for row 10. Required, and it is half of what an actionable anomaly must be able to say.

jetsa:anomaly_deviation_magnitude.description: How far out, in standard deviations or as a ratio per signal type (the proposal names it deviation_magnitude). Optional rather than required as the proposal has it: rows 4, 5 and 10 are boolean predicates with no magnitude to report.

jetsa:anomaly_confounders.description: **What the detector could not rule out** - the other half of what an actionable anomaly must say, and the per-observation form of what each detector row *cannot see*. Required; an empty list asserts that none of the fourteen applies, which is the contradicting_evidence discipline on Hypothesis reused. Has no counterpart in the proposal, which was written against a warehouse rather than against this execution record.

jetsa:anomaly_detector_ref.description: The deterministic detector that emitted this (the proposal names it detector_ref, optional; required here because the detector rows differ in what they can see and an anomaly whose detector is unknown cannot be read against the right row).

jetsa:Evidence.description: One evidence item of a Hypothesis (the proposal's evidence `$defs`): a value object in working memory, so the RCA escalation trigger — contradictory evidence exceeding supporting — is a rule-countable fact rather than a JSON blob.

jetsa:source_ref.description: A resolvable reference into the source.

jetsa:Hypothesis.description: A causal hypothesis for an Incident (the proposal's Hypothesis): the RCA agent's output contract. contradicting_evidence is required — a calibration control, not a documentation nicety (the proposal's own note). **Made a table, and it gained exactly one property to be one.** The proposal nests a hypothesis inside its incident, so nothing in the imported schema names the incident it belongs to — which is adequate for a JSON document and is not adequate for a row. `hypothesis_incident_ref` is that name and it is **required**: a hypothesis whose incident is unknown cannot be ranked against its siblings, which is what `rank` is for. The departure from the proposal is stated rather than applied silently, on Anomaly's precedent. **The parent keeps its object property and the child gains a reference, and both are correct.** `Incident.hypotheses` is what a rule traverses in working memory; `hypothesis_incident_ref` is what a query joins on. The DDL emitter resolves the redundancy in the direction relational modelling already settles — see `_table_columns`, which omits a column for an object property whose target is itself a table.

jetsa:hypothesis_incident_ref.description: The Incident this hypothesis is about. Has no counterpart in the proposal, which nests a hypothesis inside its incident rather than keying it; required here because a table needs the join its parent's array gave it for free. Class-scoped against Remediation's incident_ref.

jetsa:cause.description: The hypothesised cause (max 500 chars in the proposal).

jetsa:rank.description: The rank among the incident's hypotheses, 1-based.

jetsa:contradicting_evidence.description: The evidence against — required; empty only where the agent explicitly asserts none exists (the proposal's rule).

jetsa:hypothesis_locus.description: **The triage classifier's verdict this hypothesis was derived from** - the same nine-value vocabulary Incident.incident_locus is constrained by, deliberately not a second list. Added before the first row was written rather than after. Required: the ranker's headline finding is that 20 of 29 model-generated hypotheses sat at loci triage did not find present, and without this column a hypothesis raised at an absent locus is indistinguishable in stored data from a sound one - which would persist exactly that failure mode, in a form that hides it.

jetsa:basis.description: **How the rank was arrived at, as counts.** The requirement that a human can read a ranking's basis was met by what the ranker emits and did not survive the write; this is the column that carries it. Required, because a hypothesis whose basis is absent is one nobody can check and the whole argument for the deterministic floor is that its arithmetic is checkable.

jetsa:Incident.description: A triaged cluster of anomalies (the proposal's Incident), keyed on a session. Widened from the skeleton to what the triage design's reading of the execution record says an incident can be *about*, and made a table. The first line above is deliberately a complete sentence: the `.jr` emitter takes an entity's class comment from the docstring's first **physical** line, so a sentence that wraps is published half-written. **The widening is a grain and a locus, and both come from the record rather than from the proposal.** **The grain.** As first declared this entity had six properties — identity, classification, severity, status, model version and its hypotheses — and **none of them was a session, a run, a pipeline or a time**, so an incident could not say what it was about. Does an incident aggregate anomalies or is it one per anomaly? The record answers that it aggregates and that the key is `session_id`, because seven tables can carry evidence for an incident and `session_id` is the only key all seven share. `incident_session_id` is therefore required. **The step and shard references are optional and that is the finding, not a hedge**: localisation is a property of an incident and not its identity, evidenced where the locus supplies it and absent where it does not. **The boundary of that answer is worth keeping in view.** *One incident per session* is the grain the record can **evidence**; it is not a claim that a run produces at most one incident. Two anomalies in one session with disjoint loci are arguably two incidents and nothing in the record forbids it. What is settled is that an incident cannot be keyed *below* the session. The triage classifier decides whether to split within one. **The locus.** `incident_locus` is required and is typed against `IncidentLocus`, which is what the record actually decides; `classification` stays, typed against the imported `IncidentClassification`, which is what a diagnosis claims. Carrying both is the triage design's recommendation and it is followed here rather than resolved — see `IncidentLocus`'s docstring for why pruning the imported taxonomy is not this model's call to make. **The one thing the design did not settle is which of the two is required, and the answer follows from its own finding.** `classification` is **optional**. The record supplies a locus and never a cause, and the step between them belongs to the ranker; a required classification would make a deterministic triage step unable to write an incident without inventing a cause, which is the locus-read-as-diagnosis risk compiled into the schema. Optional is not pruning: the property and its ten values both survive, and `Anomaly` has the precedent — three of the proposal's required properties are optional there because requiring them would force a detector to invent a number. **`incident_confounders` reuses `AnomalyConfounder` deliberately.** An incident that names a step must inherit `step_label_ambiguous`, because `cpipes_step_id` is a stage location rather than a step identity. A second vocabulary saying the same thing one entity over would make a detector's qualifier and a triage step's qualifier incomparable, which is the failure the closed vocabulary was authored to prevent. Required, with an empty list asserting that none of the fourteen applies — Anomaly's own discipline. **The run reference, added 2026-09-04, is a governance property rather than a localisation one.** Every other reference on this entity says where in the *execution record* the incident sits; `incident_run_ref` says which *agent run* raised it, and it exists because `jetsapi.agent_audit` is keyed on an `AgentRun` by construction. Without it a transition on an incident reached the hash chain only when its own caller named a run, which put the human corrections a labelled population needs on the unchained side of the line — the record of the system's own reclassifications tamper-evident and the record of a person's corrections to them not. It was settled on that argument; the alternatives, a chain that accepts a null run and a separate human record, are refused rather than unconsidered. **What it does not do is make the chain unconditional**, and the residue is narrower than what it replaces rather than gone. The condition moves from *the transition names a run* to *the incident names one*, so an incident raised by a deterministic triage step is still outside the chain — but it is outside it for **every** actor rather than for humans alone, which is the property a governance record needs. **What is still not here.** The proposal's impact and generated_by blocks, which still have no consumer, and `correlation_group_id`, whose counterpart was left off Anomaly for the same reason. The rule is unchanged: a skeleton widens when something can say what its fields are for.

jetsa:incident_session_id.description: The pipeline run the incident is about - `session_id` on every table of the execution record, the only key all seven evidence-bearing tables share, and the key `purge_database` deletes by. Required: an incident aggregates anomalies and cannot be keyed below the session. Class-scoped against Anomaly's anomaly_session_id.

jetsa:incident_run_ref.description: The AgentRun that raised the incident, when one did. **This is what makes a classification transition chainable** - jetsapi.agent_audit is keyed on an AgentRun by construction, so before this property a transition could reach the hash chain only if its own caller named a run, and the callers least able to name one are the human ones the labelling instrument depends on. RecordIncidentTransition reads this off the row and uses it when the caller supplies none. **Optional, and optional is not a hedge**: the triage classifier is deterministic by design and a deterministic triage step is not an AgentRun, so an incident it raises names none and there is no honest value to invent. Class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's run_ref, AgentRun's run_id and IncidentEvent's event_run_ref; it is not incident_session_id, which is a *pipeline* session and names no agent (the naming hazard that kept the name run_ref off this entity).

jetsa:incident_detected_at.description: When the incident was raised. Class-scoped against Anomaly's detected_at, which is when a detector emitted an observation rather than when triage clustered them.

jetsa:incident_locus.description: **Where in the execution record the evidence sits** - the nine loci, the taxonomy the record can evidence and the one the triage classifier classifies deterministically. Required, and carried beside classification rather than instead of it: the locus is evidence, the classification is a claim.

jetsa:classification.description: The causal classification (the proposal's ten), kept and unpruned on the triage design's recommendation. **Optional rather than required as the proposal has it**: the record supplies a locus and never a cause, and the step from one to the other belongs to the ranker rather than the triage classifier - so a required classification would force a deterministic triage step to invent one, which is the locus-read-as-diagnosis risk written into the schema. Three of the ten have no substrate in JetStore's record at all and four are evidenced only at a grain coarser than the class name implies.

jetsa:status.description: Where the incident sits in the proposal's incident state machine.

jetsa:incident_step_ref.description: The `cpipes_step_id` the incident localises to, where the locus supplies one. Optional by construction - four of the nine loci have no step. An incident that sets it should carry step_label_ambiguous in incident_confounders.

jetsa:incident_shard_ref.description: The shard the incident localises to, where the locus supplies one. Optional for the same reason as incident_step_ref, and narrower: `shard_id` is on three of the seven evidence-bearing tables and the edge table reaches it only through its parent.

jetsa:incident_confounders.description: **What the incident's evidence could not rule out**, in the same closed vocabulary a detector writes. Required; an empty list asserts that none of the fourteen applies. step_label_ambiguous is required whenever incident_step_ref is set.

jetsa:hypotheses.description: The ranked causal hypotheses. Optional: this was once declared list[Hypothesis] with default=None, which Pydantic does not validate and which the sidecar reported as optional while the DDL emitter would have read as required - the same defect fixed twice on ChangeProposal, found here because tabling the entity is what made a column depend on the answer.

jetsa:incident_model_version.description: The proposal's domain_model_version, class-scoped: the model version the incident was raised against.

jetsa:Remediation.description: A proposed corrective action (the proposal's Remediation), a table with no executor. The first line above is deliberately one physical line: the `.jr` emitter takes an entity's class comment from the docstring's first line. **It is a table before it is a writer, and that is deliberate rather than a shortcut.** Nothing yet proposes a remediation, and nothing executes one. What the table buys is that an autonomy gate has a subject: autonomy tiers are *recorded, trustworthy, and gate nothing*, and `autonomy_tier_required` is the one property in the model that names the authority an action needs rather than the authority a run had. A tier with nowhere to be written cannot gate anything. **The one field added to the skeleton is `reversibility`, and its consumer is a constraint installed with it rather than a future caller that might want it.** The model's rule is that a skeleton widens when something can say what its fields are for; the proposal's validator rule says what this one is for, and `remediation_reversibility_ck` is where it is enforced. **That is the only property of a remediation that can be acted on without an executor** — every other gate reads what the action *does*, and what it does is the executor's to say. **Four of the proposal's nine required properties are deliberately absent, and naming them is cheaper than rediscovering them**: - `action_type` (the proposal's ten-member `RemediationActionType`) — the dispatch key. Nothing dispatches, and a tier rule keyed on it (*T2 may rerun a load and may not rotate a credential*) would be inventing the autonomy gate here. It is the first widening an executor owes. - `proposed_by` — `$ref Incident#/properties/generated_by`, the block `Incident` also does not carry, for the same reason. - `rationale` and `blast_radius` — both are read by a supervision screen deciding whether to approve, and that screen is read-only today. **`approver` and `approved_at` are absent for a different reason and it is not deferral.** `ApprovalEvent.subject_ref` is documented as *"the Remediation or ChangeProposal being decided"*, so who approved and when are already a row in `jetsapi.approval_event`. Inlining them here would be two writable statements of one fact, which is the rule `_table_columns` already applies to `Incident.hypotheses`. **The proposal's Remediation state machine and its ApprovalState do not agree, and this entity cannot fix it.** The proposal types `approval_state` against `ApprovalState`; its state machine is drawn over `proposed`, `awaiting_approval`, `executing`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `rolled_back`, `partial` and `escalated`, of which ApprovalState contains **two**. That is the divergence `lifecycle.go` recorded for ChangeProposal, where four states were missing, arriving an order of magnitude larger. **The schema is followed and the diagram is recorded**, because six of the eight missing states describe an execution nothing performs yet, and widening a controlled vocabulary for an executor that does not exist is how a model acquires fields nobody uses.

jetsa:incident_ref.description: The Incident this remediates (the proposal names it incident_id; class-scoped against Incident's identity).

jetsa:autonomy_tier_required.description: The tier the action requires (recorded; enforcement is by privilege).

jetsa:reversibility.description: Whether the action can be undone (the proposal's enum, all three values). Required, and the one field added to this skeleton: the proposal's validator rule - no irreversible remediation may be persisted at any tier - is checkable, and remediation_reversibility_ck is where it is checked. The vocabulary keeps the third member because the rule is about it.

jetsa:remediation_approval_state.description: Where the remediation sits in the approval lifecycle (the proposal names it approval_state; class-scoped against ChangeProposal's).

jetsa:DomainModelVersion.description: A released version of the domain model itself (the proposal gives its identity and intent; the fields are ours). Skeleton: the version and when it took effect.

jetsa:version.description: The semantic version of the model release.

jetsa:effective_at.description: When this version became the current one.

jetsa:IncidentEvent.description: One transition of one Incident: who moved it, when, and from what to what. The first line above is deliberately one physical line. **Ours entirely; the proposal has no counterpart, and its state machines are why it is owed.** Their preamble says *"Every transition records actor, agent version where applicable, and timestamp"* and then draws four machines and no entity to record any of them. `ApprovalEvent` is that entity for `ChangeProposal`; nothing was it for `Incident`, so a transition on an incident was a mutable `status` column and nothing else. **What that cost is a population rather than an audit trail.** Three of `IncidentStatus`'s eleven values are adjudications rather than progress — `reclassified`, `verified` and `suppressed_as_benign` — so an incident's lifecycle already carried the verdicts the four label-bearing metrics need. What it did not carry is who reached them, and **a label the measured system may have written is not a label**. There is no labelled population yet; this is the instrument that lets one accumulate. **It is a second use of the approval pattern, not a new mechanism.** `jetsapi.agent_audit` already carries an actor; `RecordApproval` already guards a transition on its expected `from_state` and writes the typed row, the chain event and the subject's new state in one transaction; `audit/lifecycle.go` already holds a transition table the server enforces and a screen reads. `audit/incident.go` and `audit/incident_lifecycle.go` are those three things again over this entity. **Three departures from `ApprovalEvent`, each with a reason.** - **`event_actor_kind` is a column, where `ApprovalEvent` leaves human and agent apart by the shape of `actor`.** See `ActorKind`: the metric partitions on kind, and a partition decided by a regular expression over an email address is not a partition. - **`classification_before` and `classification_after` travel on the event.** The incident row is mutable, so a second correction overwrites the first and the pairing the metrics score is gone. `classification_before` is **read from the row inside the write** rather than accepted from the caller (`RecordIncidentTransition`), which is the handler's *"checked against the row, not trusted as it"* rule moved down to where every caller gets it: the party being measured does not get to state what it is being measured against. - **There is no `tier_at_event`.** An approval is an authority-bearing act and an incident transition is not; the tier a *corrective action* requires is `Remediation.autonomy_tier_required`, one entity over. Stated here rather than left as an omission. **`event_run_ref` is optional, and half of the weakness that implied is gone.** `agent_audit.run_id` is `AgentRun`'s key, and neither a human working a screen nor a deterministic triage step is an `AgentRun`. While `Incident` had no run reference, a transition with no run was durable, attributable and not tamper-evident. **`Incident` now carries `incident_run_ref`** (decided 2026-09-04), and `RecordIncidentTransition` reads it off the row when the caller names no run. So this column stays optional and is now **filled from the incident for the transitions that could not fill it themselves** — a human's correction of an agent-raised incident is chained, which is the row the labelling instrument is for. What survives is that an incident raised by something that is not an `AgentRun` chains nothing, and that residue is uniform across actors rather than aimed at humans.

jetsa:event_incident_ref.description: The Incident this transition moved. Class-scoped against Remediation's incident_ref and Hypothesis's hypothesis_incident_ref; the mechanical <class>_incident_ref form would stutter here, this class name already beginning with incident.

jetsa:from_status.description: The status the incident was in. Class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's from_state, and named status rather than state because it is IncidentStatus's vocabulary and not ApprovalState's - the two machines share neither members nor shape.

jetsa:event_actor.description: Who moved it: a user_email or an agent identity, as jetsapi.agent_audit.actor and ApprovalEvent.actor carry it (class-scoped against the latter).

jetsa:event_actor_kind.description: **Whether that actor was a person or the system** - the column a labelled population needs, and the one a label-bearing metric partitions on. Required: a transition whose kind is unknown counts for nothing, so there is no honest default.

jetsa:transitioned_at.description: When the transition was made. Class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's decided_at and Incident's incident_detected_at, which is when the incident was raised rather than when it last moved.

jetsa:event_run_ref.description: The AgentRun this transition belongs to, when it has one; the chain event is appended to that run and is omitted when this is unset. **Filled from the caller when it names a run and from Incident.incident_run_ref otherwise**, so a human at a screen chains onto the run that raised the incident rather than onto nothing. Still optional, because an incident raised by something that is not an AgentRun supplies none either. Class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's run_ref.

jetsa:classification_before.description: The incident's classification before the transition, read from the row by RecordIncidentTransition rather than supplied by the caller. Null where the incident carried none - which is the ordinary case out of the triage classifier, since classification is optional and a locus is not a cause.

jetsa:classification_after.description: The classification the transition set, null where it changed none. Required in effect for a reclassification, by incident_event_reclassified_ck rather than by this annotation: the proposal says reclassified returns to triaged *with a new classification and a recorded reason*, and that is a cross-column rule.

jetsa:transition_rationale.description: Why, in the actor's words. Optional in general and required for a reclassification by the same CHECK. Class-scoped against ApprovalEvent's decision_rationale.

jetsa:HypothesisBasis.description: How a hypothesis was ranked, as numbers (decided 2026-09-04). **Numbers rather than prose, and that is the whole of the shape.** The ranker emits a sentence per hypothesis and a sentence per ranking; a sentence cannot be checked against anything, and a count can. `supporting_count` and `contradicting_count` are the lengths of the two evidence arrays on the same row, so a reader — or a test — can confirm that the stored confidence is the ratio it claims to be, months after the run and without the run. **Why it is persisted at all, which the question had to settle rather than assume.** *Reconstructable by re-running* is false for the model arm: it was measured at 16 hypotheses on one run and 13 on the next from identical input. And the evidence expires while the row persists, on two independent clocks — `RETENTION_DAYS` with no default and a hard-coded six months on the run header — so even the deterministic floor's basis is reconstructable only inside a window nobody has set.

jetsa:supporting_count.description: How many evidence items were for the hypothesis. The length of supporting_evidence on the same row, stored so that the ratio confidence claims can be checked without the run.

jetsa:contradicting_count.description: How many were against. Zero is a claim the ranker made, not a question it was never asked - contradicting_evidence is required and nil fails validation.

jetsa:evidenceability.description: What the triage design says the record can do for this hypothesis's cause class. It is the ranker's primary sort key rather than a gloss: a class the substrate cannot speak to outranks nothing, whatever its counts.

AutonomyTier.description: The proposal's tier vocabulary. Lexicographic order is tier order — the tier-ceiling comparisons work on the text directly, so do not relabel the tiers with descriptive names and do not exceed T9.

AnomalySubject.description: The proposal's Anomaly `subject_ref.entity_type` — what an anomaly is *about*. **The first six are the proposal's; the last two are the detectors' two grains.** The execution record's rows are per *worker* (run × step label × shard × `jets_partition`) and per *edge* (worker × input channel × output channel), and neither is one of the six. `stage` is the near miss and is not the same thing: `cpipes_step_id` is a stage location, but a worker is finer than a stage by shard and partition, and an edge is finer again. Added with the SignalType additions above, on the same terms.

SignalType.description: The proposal's Anomaly `$defs` — scoped to Anomaly and, like EvidenceSource, not in the proposal's vocabulary list. **The first ten are the proposal's, verbatim and in its order. The last three are ours**, added because the ten do not name three of the six failure modes the anomaly design found derivable from JetStore's execution record, and `signal_type` is required by the proposal — so without them an anomaly for those rows is unrepresentable rather than merely unlabelled. The ten were written for a warehouse's data-quality signals (volume, freshness, distribution, cardinality); the detector rows are *execution* signals, which is a different substrate rather than a gap in the proposal. Of the ten, the detectors populate exactly two today: `rejection_rate` is row 1 and `volume` is rows 2 and 5. **The anomaly detectors confirm or overturn the three additions** — they are the first caller that has to choose a value.

AnomalyConfounder.description: **Ours entirely, and it is the vocabulary form of what each detector row *cannot see*** (14 values). Not in the proposal at any level. The anomaly design is the reason it exists: every derivable row needs at least one qualifier carried with the anomaly, or it is not actionable — an `Anomaly` that cannot say what it compared against and what it could not rule out reproduces the signal an operator learns to ignore. `basis` carries the first half; this carries the second. **A member is an alternative explanation the detector could not exclude, or a bound on the comparison it made** — not a defect, and not a reason to suppress the anomaly. Each is traceable to one detector row, named in the comment beside it; **the list is appended to, never renumbered**. It is deliberately *not* free text. A named `text` literal makes a mistyped value a compile error rather than a comparison that silently never matches (the .jr emitter's own argument), and free text would make two detectors' qualifiers incomparable, which defeats the purpose.

EvidenceSource.description: The proposal's Hypothesis evidence `$defs` — scoped to Evidence and deliberately NOT in the proposal's vocabulary list, which is why the emitters discover vocabularies by reachability (10 values, 9 of them the proposal's). **The first nine are the proposal's; the tenth is ours.** Read against what JetStore actually has, two are unconditional, four are conditional or partial, and **three had no substrate at all** — `commit_history` (no run names a commit), `infrastructure_log` (what the record holds is a decoded `StoppedReason` string, not a log) and `prior_incident`, the last of which stops being substrate-less once `jetsapi.incident` exists. That vocabulary is therefore **too wide** for the record, the mirror of SignalType, which was too narrow; the honest response is to say so rather than to prune an imported model unilaterally, so nothing is removed here. **What is added is a member for evidence that already exists and had nowhere to be filed.** `AnomalyConfounder`'s fourteen members are the record's own statement of what a detector could not rule out, they are a closed vocabulary, and every anomaly the detectors write already carries them. That is contradicting evidence in the record's own words, and the proposal's nine sources have no member for it — so the ranker's hardest requirement, the contradicting side of a ranked hypothesis, had a populated substrate and no way to name it. `detector_confounder` is that name, and it is an **addition** rather than a re-derivation.

IncidentClassification.description: The proposal's causal taxonomy of an incident (10 values).

IncidentLocus.description: **Ours entirely, and it is the taxonomy the triage design derived from the execution record** (9 values). Not in the proposal at any level. **A locus is where in the record a cause would have to have left its evidence; it is not a cause.** The triage design's finding is that the record supports triage and does not support root-cause attribution below the level of a hypothesis. The nine below are mutually distinguishable by predicates over `jetsapi` with no free-text parsing and no join outside it, and eight of the nine are computable in SQL. **Both vocabularies are carried, on the triage design's recommendation.** `IncidentClassification` above says what *produced* the failure and three of its ten members have no substrate in JetStore at all; pruning an imported model unilaterally is not this model's call. So `classification` stays typed against the proposal's ten and `incident_locus` is added beside it. **The locus is evidence and the classification is a claim**, which is the distinction the anomaly design drew between an anomaly's observation and its basis. **The risk this vocabulary creates** is that a nine-member locus taxonomy sitting beside a ten-member cause taxonomy will be read as a second cause taxonomy, and *classified* will be read as *diagnosed*. The member names are written as observations rather than as diagnoses for that reason — `worker_not_terminated` and not `worker_hung`, `rows_lost_silently` and not `data_dropped`. Ordered by how early the failure occurs, which is also roughly the order of how little the record retains. Appended to, never renumbered.

IncidentStatus.description: The proposal's incident lifecycle (11 values), and its state machine.

Reversibility.description: The proposal's Remediation `reversibility` enum (3 values), verbatim and in its order. **The DDL accepts two of the three, and that is the proposal's own validator rule rather than a pruning.** The appendix states it in terms: *"`reversibility: irreversible` is rejected at schema level. No irreversible remediation may be persisted at any tier (Section 4.3)."* The vocabulary keeps all three — the third is what the rule is *about*, and a vocabulary that omitted it could not express the rule — and `remediation_reversibility_ck` is where the refusal happens. A stated invariant that is checkable and left in prose is one that goes quiet the first time nobody re-reads the appendix. The excluded member is read off this enum rather than spelled into the SQL, so a rename moves the rule instead of silently stopping it from firing.

ActorKind.description: **Ours entirely** (2 values). Not in the proposal at any level. **Who made a transition, as a column rather than as a spelling convention.** `ApprovalEvent.actor` and `jetsapi.agent_audit.actor` both carry *"a user_email or an agent identity"* and leave the two apart by the shape of the string. That is adequate for attribution — the question those columns were built to answer is *which* actor — and it is not adequate for the question a labelled population asks, which is *which kind*. **A label the measured system may have written is not a label**: the label-bearing metrics score an agent's classification against a human's correction, so a query that cannot partition the corrections by kind has no denominator. Deciding that by pattern-matching an email address would make the population a property of a regular expression. Two members and no more. `agent` covers a deterministic classifier as well as a model-driven one: the distinction that matters to a metric is whether the transition came from **outside** the system under test, and the triage classifier being deterministic does not put it outside.

Evidenceability.description: **Ours entirely** (5 values): the triage design's evidenceability reading reduced to a vocabulary. Not in the proposal at any level. The triage design asked, per imported cause class, *can the record evidence this class*, and answered in prose per cell. The ranker reduced those answers to five tiers and **sorts on them as its primary key** — a class the substrate cannot speak to is not a weak candidate, which is the finding that inverted its first ranking. The tier is therefore an input to a rank rather than a gloss on one, and it is persisted for that reason. The order below is the sort order: better-evidenced first.
